executive_summary: The analysis of four documents reveals a fundamental tension between official accounts of the Brumaire coup—the decree, proclamation, and constitution—and Bourrienne's memoir. While the official texts present the change of authority as a lawful, necessary act grounded in revolutionary values, Bourrienne's behind-the-scenes narrative emphasizes the coup's contingent nature, the personal deceptions involved, and Napoleon Bonaparte's flawed public performance at St. Cloud. Together, these sources show that the same event can be portrayed as both a formal legal transfer and a high-risk personal enterprise, with no claim of consistency between the two genres.
key_findings: The official documents (the Brumaire decree and the Year VIII Constitution) establish the change of authority through formal legal mechanisms: the creation of a provisional consular commission (A0017) and the appointment of three consuls for ten years (A0002).

Bourrienne's memoir directly contradicts any official or later narrative that Bonaparte delivered a coherent speech at St. Cloud, stating that his remarks were confused and devoid of dignity and sense (A0010, A0012).

The memoir emphasizes the contingent nature of the coup, suggesting that failure and even Bonaparte's execution were real possibilities (A0009, A0013), in contrast to the official documents' tone of necessity and inevitability.

Bourrienne's narrative details specific strategic deceptions, such as Bonaparte sending him to deceive Barras by pretending to have a headache (A0004, A0005), which are absent from the formal legal record.
cross_cutting_patterns: The memoir's claim that Bonaparte's speech was incoherent and that the coup was contingent directly undermines the official documents' presentation of the event as a necessary, lawfully executed change of authority justified by republican principles.

actionable_recommendations.title: Expand the corpus to include additional contemporary memoirs and official speech texts
actionable_recommendations.description: To fully map the divergence between official and memoir accounts, this analysis should be extended to include the full text of revolutionary-era speeches (e.g., Bonaparte's alleged St. Cloud addresses) and other contemporary memoirs (e.g., Barras’s or Sieyès’s) that can corroborate or challenge Bourrienne’s specific claim that no coherent speech was delivered.

actionable_recommendations.title: Increase textual coverage within existing document types
actionable_recommendations.description: Apply the same coding scheme to the full text of Bourrienne's memoir and the complete organic laws of the Year VIII Constitution to verify whether the observed pattern of legal formality versus contingent personal narrative holds consistently across larger samples.

actionable_recommendations.title: Investigate the dissemination and reception of official documents
actionable_recommendations.description: Analyze the specific audiences and publication contexts of the decree, proclamation, and constitution (e.g., were they posted publicly, read aloud, or archived?) to understand the intended reach and rhetorical effect of the official version of events, which this corpus alone does not reveal.

confidence_assessment.evidence: Direct, explicit textual evidence from the memoir that Bonaparte's speech was confused, incoherent, and stammered – supported by application references A0010 and A0012. The official documents provide no counter-narrative of the speech's content.

Multiple passages in the memoir (A0009, A0013) explicitly state that success was not inevitable and that failure could have led to Bonaparte's execution. This is robust internal evidence from a single source.

The official documents (A0017, A0002) clearly establish the legal framework of the new consular government. The contrast with Bourrienne’s narrative is structurally clear, though the legal texts do not directly address the execution events.

analytical_memo: A key analytical decision was to treat Bourrienne's claim that no coherent speech was delivered at St. Cloud as a direct contradiction of any official narrative that later attributed formal speeches to Bonaparte—this was supported by the explicit memoir text. A surprise was the degree to which Bourrienne's account of contingency (e.g., the risk of Bonaparte's execution) was supported by multiple passages and directly contrasted with the official documents' tone of inevitable necessity. Uncertainty remains about whether Bourrienne's memoir represents a corrective or a self-serving reinterpretation, and about the precise audience and reception of the official documents; these areas warrant further investigation with additional sources.
